Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-03
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Trisha Nunez (Redwood AE), Marco Li (Redwood SE), Sandra Ortiz (CISO, HelixHealth), Ben Kline (Infra Lead), Aisha Rahman (Compliance Manager)

Auto-generated sections (may contain errors):
Summary: See above.
Topics: audit logs, exports, retention, RBAC, KMS
Action items: listed below.

Transcript:
[00:00] Trisha: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Sandra: Sandra here, hi.
[00:07] Ben: Ben, yep.
[00:09] Aisha: Aisha here.
[00:12] Trisha: Great. Marco from infra side at Redwood is here and we'll walk through audit logging specifics, particularly admin activity.
[00:18] Marco: Hey all. Quick note, I'm going to share my screen in a minute, but first want to scope what you need to see.
[00:25] Ben: We're primarily concerned about two things: one, what admin actions are logged (user creation, API key ops, role changes), and two, how we get those logs into our SIEM and store them for the required retention.
[00:36] Trisha: Yep that's what we planned for. Also Sandra, you mentioned SOC 2 evidence - we can show where audit logs live and how retention is configured.
[00:43] Sandra: Correct. For audits we need immutable evidence of admin activity, and proof that only authorized folks can view/download logs.
[00:50] Marco: Good. Quick overview: Redwood captures three tiers of events for admin activity: console UI events, API and control-plane events, and background system events (automatic role sync, auth token rotation). Examples: user create/delete, role/grant changes, SSO link/unlink, API key create/delete/rotate, model version rollouts, config changes to retention or routing policies.
[01:15] (Speaker 1): The transcript sometimes garbles product names, so you might see res-west vs reswest, e.g.
[01:22] Sandra: Can you say if the logs include before/after state for role changes?
[01:26] Marco: Short answer: yes. We capture pre-change and post-change snapshots for a lot of admin ops. It's in the admin_event object as state_before/state_after in the JSON export.
[01:36] Ben: Is that included in the default retention? Or is state diffs an opt-in?
[01:40] Marco: Default export includes metadata and state diffs for admin ops for 90 days in hosted plans. For Dedicated/Private you can configure longer retention or ship to external storage.
[01:49] Aisha: Our regulator requires 7 years for some artifacts. How do you support legal-hold/archival?
[01:55] Trisha: Two patterns: 1) long-term export to S3 with server-side encryption using customer KMS keys (you keep CMKs), and 2) stream to SIEMs (Splunk/Datadog/Elastic) which then apply your retention/immutability policies. We also support write-once storage via object lock on S3 for immutability if you manage the bucket settings.
[02:18] Sandra: About encryption: can Redwood encrypt logs at rest with customer-managed keys? Or do you only use Redwood KMS?
[02:25] Marco: Both. For exports we support SSE-KMS with your key. For logs stored in Redwood's control plane we use our managed KMS, but we have an option to use your KMIP/HSM or bring-your-own-KMS in Private deployments. In Dedicated we can configure key wrapping with your KMS.
[02:40] Ben: When you say "log export", is that a full dump or continuous streaming?
[02:44] Marco: Options: immediate ad-hoc export (NDJSON), scheduled daily full export, or continuous streaming via Kinesis/Kafka/HTTPS forwarder to Splunk/Datadog. You can also do S3 async push which is useful for long-term archiving.
[02:58] Sandra: What about Timestamps and timezones? Need them all in UTC for forensics.
[03:02] Marco: All Redwood audit timestamps are in RFC3339 UTC. There is also a created_at and event_time field for each record.
[03:10] (Speaker 2): Minor mis-transcription: some customers see timezone tags as Zulu or +00:00, they're equivalent.
[03:16] Aisha: Do the logs include IP addresses and actor identity (like SAML subject, email)?
[03:20] Marco: Yes. Each event has actor_identity with SSO subject, user email, user_id, and source_ip. For system automated actions the actor_identity is the system service principal.
[03:28] Ben: Are admin credential rotations (API keys) captured? We need to see key create/delete/rotate and who performed it.
[03:33] Marco: Yes, key lifecycle events are captured including key fingerprints. We do not include full secret values in logs.
[03:40] Sandra: How easy is it to search logs? Do you provide a UI for filtering admin events?
[03:45] Marco: In Console -> Observability -> Audit Logs you can filter by event type, actor, resource, time range. We also provide export API to run queries and return NDJSON. For large-scale search we recommend streaming into your SIEM.
[03:58] Trisha: Also want to call out RBAC restrictions: viewing raw audit logs requires the "Audit Viewer" role; only Admin+Compliance roles can request exports.
[04:07] Aisha: Can you enforce separation of duties? Eg, infra team can read runtime logs but only compliance can export admin logs.
[04:12] Marco: Yes, RBAC is hierarchical and supports attribute-based policies. You can create a role that allows read-only console access but not exports.
[04:20] Ben: On the export format: NDJSON vs CSV? Which fields are guaranteed?
[04:25] Marco: Standard export is NDJSON. Each line is a JSON event with a stable schema: event_id, event_type, resource_type, resource_id, actor_identity, state_before, state_after, metadata, event_time, received_time, region, request_id. CSV is available for simplified exports but it flattens nested state fields, so NDJSON is recommended.
[04:43] Sandra: For audits we need cryptographic verification that logs haven't been tampered with. Does Redwood support signing exported files?
[04:50] Marco: We provide two mechanisms: 1) server-side signing of export bundles with Redwood's signing key (we can provide the public key for verification), and 2) you can configure Lambda to compute checksums/hashes on the S3 bucket on arrival, or use object tagging. For higher assurance we recommend S3 Object Lock + server-side encryption + signed manifests.
[05:07] Aisha: Is the signing key auditable? We need chain-of-custody docs.
[05:11] Marco: We can supply key rotation logs and we publish a KMS access audit that shows which Redwood principals used the signing key. For Private deployments customers can host signing keys entirely inside their HSM.
[05:23] Trisha: There's a frequent question about how long we keep logs in the control plane by default. For Hosted it's 90 days; Dedicated starts at 1 year by default but is configurable; Private is under your control.
[05:34] Ben: Does retention deletion follow hard deletion or soft-delete? We need forensically sound deletion policies.
[05:39] Marco: We use soft-delete (tombstone) for a short grace period to recover from accidental deletion, then hard-delete per retention policy. For compliance you can disable the grace period in Dedicated/Private.
[05:51] (background noise)
[05:55] Sandra: Auditors ask for export runbooks. Can you provide example playbooks for producing evidence for X months?
[06:01] Trisha: Yes, we'll share runbooks and an export checklist. We'll also provide example queries to prove admin events for a time window.
[06:08] Ben: On SIEM integration, any native connector? Splunk HEC, Datadog logs, and syslog?
[06:14] Marco: Native connectors: Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs ingestion, HTTP endpoints for generic webhooks, Kafka/Kinesis, and S3. We also have a syslog forwarder for on-prem SIEM ingestion.
[06:26] Aisha: Data residency: can logs be stored only in EU regions? We have EU-only rules.
[06:32] Marco: Yes, you can configure export region or choose regional storage endpoints. For Hosted we have EU region buckets and the control plane can be configured to route logs to EU S3. For Private on-prem we of course keep data on-prem.
[06:45] Sandra: For access to logs inside Redwood console, is the traffic encrypted end-to-end and do you log who viewed logs?
[06:52] Marco: All console traffic is TLS; access to view/download logs is itself an auditable event and we log log_access events. Those include the viewer identity, method (console/API), and the resource.
[07:05] Ben: Do you redact sensitive fields in logs, e.g., PII, or is that left to customers?
[07:10] Marco: By default we avoid logging request payloads that contain user content. Admin logs do include identifiers like usernames and emails, but you can configure redaction rules on export or during streaming. We also provide a log-filtering stage to mask or drop fields before they leave our system.
[07:26] Trisha: Quick Q from my side: how would you like the sample evidence delivered? NDJSON vs Splunk HEC demo?
[07:31] Sandra: NDJSON sample plus a quick Splunk HEC forwarder demo would be great.
[07:35] Trisha: Noted. Marco will produce the samples.
[07:38] Marco: I'll produce a 24hr sample NDJSON, plus a small pipeline demo pushing to Splunk HEC.
[07:43] (interrupt)
[07:45] Aisha: We also need retention proof: screenshots of retention config, plus an export showing state_before/state_after for a role change.
[07:52] Marco: We'll include that.
[07:54] Sandra: A question about alerts: can we configure alerts on admin events (like API key deletion)?
[07:58] Marco: Yes, you can create alerting rules in Console -> Observability -> Alerts that trigger on specific event_type patterns and forward to PagerDuty/Slack/Email or call a webhook.
[08:07] Ben: Is there rate-limiting on export or streaming? We might have high-volume events during bulk ops.
[08:12] Marco: Streams are throughput-based. For large bursts we buffer to S3 then forward. We also provide backpressure mechanisms and retries. For Dedicated instances we can bump throughput with reserved capacity.
[08:24] Trisha: Ok I'm going to share a sample schema on screen, bear with me.
[08:28] (screen-share started)
[08:30] Marco: Schema highlights: event_type: ADMIN_USER_CREATE, ADMIN_ROLE_UPDATE, API_KEY_ROTATE; metadata includes request_id, correlation_id; state_before/state_after canonicalized.
[08:40] Sandra: Do you include correlation IDs for cross-service tracing?
[08:44] Marco: Yes we add correlation_id for actions triggered by user flows so auditors can piece together sequences.
[08:51] Ben: Example: If we rotate keys and then run a deploy, can we link those?
[08:55] Marco: Correlation ID plus request_id should allow linking in most cases; for multi-step workflows we also surface parent_event_id.
[09:03] (15:00 mark - note timestamps in real call continued roughly)
[09:06] Aisha: About audit log integrity - how do we handle replays or duplicate events when streaming to SIEM?
[09:11] Marco: Each event has a monotonically increasing sequence and an event_id UUID. Consumers should dedupe on event_id. Our streaming client also supports exactly-once delivery semantics when writing to compatible sinks (eg, Kinesis with sequence tokens).
[09:24] Sandra: For forensics we may need chain-of-custody for log exports. What's in the manifest when you publish an export?
[09:30] Marco: The export manifest includes export_id, start_time, end_time, event_count, checksum (SHA256) for the bundle, signer_public_key, retention_policy_id, and region.
[09:38] Ben: Do you support field-level encryption for exported logs?
[09:42] Marco: We support envelope encryption: you can request that certain sensitive fields be encrypted with a field-specific key that you manage. That needs to be configured up-front.
[09:50] Trisha: Time for a quick recap and next steps?
[09:53] Sandra: Yes please.
[09:54] Trisha: Recap: Redwood logs admin activity with before/after state, includes actor identity and IPs, supports NDJSON exports and continuous streaming to SIEMs, supports SSE-KMS with customer keys for S3 exports, offers signing/manifests and object-lock options for immutability, RBAC to restrict log viewing and export, and retention is configurable (Hosted 90d default).
[10:16] Aisha: That matches our notes. We'll validate retention length and legal-hold needs.
[10:20] Trisha: Next steps: Marco will produce NDJSON sample and Splunk HEC demo; I'll send SOC2/ISO attestation blurb and retention configuration docs; Aisha to confirm retention window.
[10:30] Ben: One last question - do exports contain internal request IDs that might reveal infra details? We want minimal leak of internal topology.
[10:36] Marco: We can redact internal hostnames and include only minimal request IDs; the default includes request_id but not internal host identifiers. For tighter controls we can filter them out.
[10:44] Sandra: Great. If possible add a short appendix to the runbook about redact options.
[10:48] Trisha: Will do.
[10:50] (closing)
[10:51] Trisha: Thanks everyone, expect artifacts in the next 48 hours.
[10:54] Sandra: Thanks.
[10:55] Ben: Thanks all.
[10:56] (call ends)
